title: I went to the Anthropic IPO protest in NYC. Where was everybody?
excerpt: Journalists outnumbered protesters outside the Nasdaq on the morning of Anthropic's IPO. It reminded me: AI isn't a top-of-mind issue for most.
content_html:
By Henry Chandonnet

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-19T21:17:20.522Z

The protesters outside the Nasdaq were loud, passionate — and few in number.

Anthropic went public on Thursday morning, dumping even more money into the AI trade and making its cofounders filthy rich. For some, it was cause for celebration. For those who think that AI will obliterate the job market, create humanity-destroying diseases, or end the world, it was time to pick up the bullhorn.

I arrived at the Nasdaq on Thursday morning, ready for anything. At 9 a.m. on the dot, a handful of protesters unfurled big red signs. More soon joined, growing to what I'd estimate was 30 activists.

And yet, across from the protesters was a swarm of photographers that was double (if not triple) the protesters' size. One of the activists told me that he kept accidentally giving the buttons he made to journalists, because there were just so many of them there.

What's with the imbalance? It says something about the state of the AI backlash — and how people actually feel about these massive, cash-guzzling companies.

Meet the Anthropic IPO protesters

There was a bit of idea mush at the Anthropic IPO protest.

Activists had different reasons for opposing AI development. Some came from the Jacob Coxon school of "AI is going to end the world." Others were specifically focused on healthcare, climate, or data centers.

The organizations present were equally sprawling, from Climate Defiance to the Democratic Socialists of America to the AIDS activists of ACT UP. They united under a hashtag: #StopTechOligarchs.

Some opposed the IPO, including an early speaker who said the AI bubble was worse than the 2008 financial crisis. Ian Lund, a 31-year-old from Massachusetts who works in the climate sector, said that the IPO brought the personal consequences into focus.

"I'm probably invested in it now, through my 401(k)," Lund said. "I didn't want to assume that risk."

Others were indifferent to Anthropic's financial milestone. Newly sworn-in state senator Aber Kawas from New York told me that IPOs were "something that happens." She was more interested in reducing AI use in the wars in Gaza and Iran.

Many were in leadership positions at AI slowdown organizations, such as Lund, who cofounded the New York Tech Accountability Project. Bryce Rogers and Megan Lagerquist are on the leadership team of the Resisting Automated Disempowerment collective.

Rogers wasn't always so worried about AI. "When I first heard people talking about it as a risk, I was like, 'Bro, touch grass,'" he said. Then he read up on it, saw the "dangerous trajectory," and started doing grassroots organizing in 2025.

After the protest, Rogers was headed back to his engineering job. ("My job's kind of flexible," he said of the early-morning hours.) Lagerquist was going shopping for a wedding dress.

AI isn't a top-of-mind issue

All of the protesters that I spoke to used AI in some form, like summarizing articles and writing code. These weren't the "never-AI" heads; they merely wanted a slowdown.

Let's face it: slowdowns aren't sexy. It's easier to market a boycott than it is to consider thoughtful regulation.

And, while Americans don't feel great about AI or data centers or the slop that covers their Facebook feeds, it's not a top-of-mind problem. Only 30% of Americans surveyed told Gallup that AI data centers were "extremely important" to their vote ahead of the midterm elections, outranked by issues like immigration, abortion, and the conflict between Israel and Palestine.

There was one big point of action: police detainments. Four of the protesters sat themselves in front of the Nasdaq doors, inching closer and closer until the cops came and cuffed them. That was over an hour in, at which point most of the protesters had left.

So no, New Yorkers weren't racing to protest Anthropic's big day. San Francisco's protest were bigger, but that's where everyone — and I mean everyone — is talking, thinking, and catastrophizing about AI. The philosopher king Coxon was there to speak, too.

Even Lund's 35-year-old cofounder passed. He told him: "You go to the protest today. I'm too old."
